items.stem: What is meant by “ammonotelism”?
items.answer: The process of excreting ammonia, seen in many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the process of excreting ammonia, seen in many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as ureotelic animal or uricotelic animal: mammals, reptiles, insects, marine fishes.
items.answer: mammals – ureotelic animal; reptiles – uricotelic animal; insects – uricotelic animal; marine fishes – ureotelic animal.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: mammals – ureotelic animal; reptiles – uricotelic animal; insects – uricotelic animal; marine fishes – ureotelic animal.

kidneys

items.stem: A part of the human nephron or kidney has these features: receives filtrate from many nephrons; opens into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids; large amounts of water can be reabsorbed here. Identify the part. Give a reason.

items.markingKey: 1 mark: the collecting duct; 1 mark: the features receives filtrate from many nephrons; opens into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids; large amounts of water can be reabsorbed here are characteristic of it.

items.stem:
A fish in a river near Patna, a frog on land and a sparrow eliminate their nitrogenous wastes in different forms.
(i) In which form does each excrete its nitrogenous waste? (1 mark)
(ii) Which form is the most toxic and which needs the least water? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how the habitat determines the form of waste excreted. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Fish – ammonia (ammonotelic); terrestrial frog – urea (ureotelic); sparrow – uric acid (uricotelic). (ii) Ammonia most toxic; uric acid needs the least water. (iii) Aquatic animals have plenty of water to dilute and diffuse toxic ammonia; terrestrial animals must conserve water and convert ammonia to less toxic urea or uric acid.

protonephridia (flame cells)

items.stem: Give two differences between the proximal convoluted tubule and the loop of Henle.
items.answer: The proximal convoluted tubule: highly coiled; major site of reabsorption. The loop of Henle: dips into the medulla; hairpin-shaped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. the proximal convoluted tubule – highly coiled; major site of reabsorption; the loop of Henle – dips into the medulla; hairpin-shaped.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as excretory structure of invertebrates or excretory structure of vertebrates: Malpighian tubules, kidneys, protonephridia (flame cells).
items.answer: Malpighian tubules – excretory structure of invertebrates; kidneys – excretory structure of vertebrates; protonephridia (flame cells) – excretory structure of invertebrates.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: Malpighian tubules – excretory structure of invertebrates; kidneys – excretory structure of vertebrates; protonephridia (flame cells) – excretory structure of invertebrates.

items.stem: Explain the term “vasa recta”.
items.answer: A minute vessel of the capillary network that runs parallel to the loop of Henle, forming a U shape.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a minute vessel of the capillary network that runs parallel to the loop of Henle, forming a U shape.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the loop of Henle and the collecting duct on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A part of the human nephron or kidney has these features: hairpin-shaped. Identify the part – the loop of Henle or the collecting duct? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) The loop of Henle: hairpin-shaped; has descending and ascending limbs; dips into the medulla. The collecting duct: receives filtrate from many nephrons; extends from the cortex to the inner medulla; opens into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids. (b) The loop of Henle.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: the loop of Henle; 1 mark: “hairpin-shaped” is a feature of the loop of Henle.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about modes of excretion and the human excretory system is correct?
items.answer: Each human kidney is 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick and weighs 120–170 g.
items.markingKey: (d) Each human kidney is 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick and weighs 120–170 g. The other statements are false. Birds are uricotelic; mammals are ureotelic. The loop of Henle dips into the medulla. Earthworms have nephridia; Malpighian tubules are found in insects including cockroaches.
options: Malpighian tubules are the excretory organs of earthworms.
Birds are ureotelic.
The loop of Henle is located in the cortex.
Each human kidney is 10–12 cm long, 5–7 cm wide, 2–3 cm thick and weighs 120–170 g.

items.stem: Define the term “counter-current mechanism”.
items.answer: The mechanism in which filtrate in the two limbs of Henle's loop and blood in the vasa recta flow in opposite directions, creating an increasing osmolarity towards the inner medulla.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the mechanism in which filtrate in the two limbs of Henle's loop and blood in the vasa recta flow in opposite directions, creating an increasing osmolarity towards the inner medulla.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about urine formation and the counter-current mechanism is correct?
items.answer: Nearly 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.
items.markingKey: (c) Nearly 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules. The other statements are false. GFR is about 125 mL per minute, i.e. about 180 litres per day. Small amounts of urea enter the thin ascending limb and are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule, adding to the gradient. Glucose, amino acids and Na⁺ are reabsorbed actively; nitrogenous wastes passively.
options: The GFR in a healthy individual is about 125 mL per day.
Urea is not involved in the medullary osmotic gradient.
Nearly 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.
Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed passively.

items.stem: Give two differences between the proximal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct.
items.answer: The proximal convoluted tubule: reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients; secretes H⁺ and ammonia and absorbs HCO₃⁻. The collecting duct: maintains pH by secretion of H⁺ and K⁺; allows passage of small amounts of urea into the interstitium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. the proximal convoluted tubule – reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients; secretes H⁺ and ammonia and absorbs HCO₃⁻; the collecting duct – maintains pH by secretion of H⁺ and K⁺; allows passage of small amounts of urea into the interstitium.

items.answer: (i) 172.8 L per day; (ii) 99.3%

items.answer: (i) The collecting duct (ii) helps produce concentrated urine (iii) impermeable to water; filtrate gets diluted as it moves up

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the proximal convoluted tubule on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A region of the renal tubule is described: NaCl added to the interstitium. Identify the region – the ascending limb of the loop of Henle or the proximal convoluted tubule? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) The ascending limb of the loop of Henle: impermeable to water; electrolytes transported actively or passively; filtrate gets diluted as it moves up. The proximal convoluted tubule: simple cuboidal brush border epithelium; reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients; reabsorbs 70–80% of electrolytes and water. (b) The ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: the ascending limb of the loop of Henle; 1 mark: “NaCl added to the interstitium” is a feature of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

items.stem: Describe the counter-current mechanism and explain how it helps to concentrate urine.
items.answer: Two limbs of Henle's loop and the vasa recta carry fluid in opposite directions; descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb impermeable to water but transports NaCl; NaCl from the ascending limb is exchanged with the descending limb of vasa recta and returned to the interstitium by its ascending portion; small amounts of urea enter the thin ascending limb and return to the interstitium from the collecting tubule; gradient from 300 to 1200 mOsmolL⁻¹; water leaves the collecting duct into the hypertonic interstitium; urine up to four times concentrated.
items.markingKey: 3 marks mechanism; 2 marks concentration of urine.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of events in urine formation: tubular reabsorption, tubular secretion, glomerular filtration. Give a reason.
items.answer: glomerular filtration → tubular reabsorption → tubular secretion
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order glomerular filtration → tubular reabsorption → tubular secretion; 1 mark for the reason: Filtration produces the filtrate; most of it is reabsorbed, and some ions are secreted.

items.stem:
After a long cricket match on a hot day in Nagpur, Sahil sweated a lot, drank little water and passed only a small volume of dark yellow urine.
(i) Which hormone increased his water reabsorption? (1 mark)
(ii) From where is it released? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how a fall in blood pressure would activate the renin-angiotensin mechanism. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) ADH (vasopressin). (ii) Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary), on signals from hypothalamic osmoreceptors. (iii) A fall in GFR/blood pressure activates JG cells to release renin; renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and then angiotensin II, which constricts vessels, raises BP and GFR, and stimulates aldosterone, increasing Na⁺ and water reabsorption.

items.stem:
A patient with failed kidneys in a hospital in Bhopal is put on an artificial kidney three times a week.
(i) What is this procedure called? (1 mark)
(ii) Why is heparin added to the blood and anti-heparin added before it returns? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how urea is removed from the blood in the machine. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Haemodialysis. (ii) Heparin prevents clotting in the machine; anti-heparin restores normal clotting before blood returns to the body. (iii) Blood passes through a coiled cellophane tube bathed in dialysing fluid that has the same composition as plasma except nitrogenous wastes; urea diffuses out along the concentration gradient.

items.stem: Describe uremia, renal calculi and glomerulonephritis. Explain haemodialysis and kidney transplantation.
items.answer: Uremia – urea accumulates in blood due to kidney malfunction; renal calculi – stones of crystallised salts (oxalates); glomerulonephritis – inflammation of glomeruli. Haemodialysis – blood from artery + heparin → dialysing unit with cellophane tube and dialysing fluid (plasma-like, no N-wastes) → urea diffuses out → anti-heparin → vein. Transplantation – ultimate correction of acute renal failure; donor preferably close relative to minimise rejection.
items.markingKey: 3 marks disorders; 2 marks treatment.
